At that time the monks from the group of six wore sandals with blue straps, yellow straps, red straps, magenta straps, black straps, orange straps, and beige straps. People complained and criticized them, “They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 2.2.6)
“You shouldn’t wear sandals with blue straps, yellow straps, red straps, magenta straps, black straps, orange straps, or beige straps. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 2.3.1)

At that time the monks from the group of six wore sandals containing leather, enclosing the shin and the foot, covering the foot, stuffed with cotton, looking like partridge feathers, having straps like ram horns, having straps like goat horns, having straps like scorpion claws, decorated with a peacock’s tail feather, and decorated in various ways. People complained and criticized them, “They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 2.3.5)

“You shouldn’t wear sandals containing leather, enclosing the shin and the foot, covering the foot, stuffed with cotton, looking like partridge feathers, having straps like ram horns, having straps like goat horns, having straps like scorpion claws, decorated with a peacock’s tail feather, or decorated in various ways. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 2.4.1)

At that time the monks from the group of six wore sandals decorated with lionskin, tiger skin, leopard skin, deerskin, otter skin, cat skin, squirrel skin, and bat skin. People complained and criticized them, “They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 2.4.5)
“You shouldn’t wear sandals decorated with lionskin, tiger skin, leopard skin, deerskin, otter skin, cat skin, squirrel skin, or bat skin. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 3.1.1)

One morning the Buddha robed up, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for almsfood together with an attendant monk. As the attendant followed behind the Buddha, he was limping. A certain lay follower wearing sandals with multi-layered soles saw the Buddha coming. He removed his sandals, approached the Buddha, and bowed. He then bowed to the attendant monk and asked him, “Venerable, why are you limping?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 3.2.2)
“Because my feet are cracked.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 3.2.3)
“Well then, take these sandals.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 3.2.4)
“Thanks, but the Buddha has prohibited sandals with multi-layered soles.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 3.2.5)
But the Buddha said, “Please take the sandals.” Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 3.2.7)
“I allow second-hand sandals with multi-layered soles. But you shouldn’t wear new sandals with multi-layered soles. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 4.1.1)

On one occasion the Buddha was doing walking meditation outside without sandals. The senior monks followed his example, but not the monks from the group of six. The monks of few desires complained and criticized them, “How can the monks from the group of six do walking meditation with their sandals on when the Teacher and the senior monks do it without?” They told the Buddha. … “Is it true, monks, that the monks from the group of six do this?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 4.2.3)
“It’s true, sir.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 4.2.4)

The Buddha rebuked them … “How can those foolish men do walking meditation with their sandals on when the Teacher and the senior monks do it without? Even the householders who wear white are respectful and deferential toward their teachers for teaching them the profession by which they make a living. And you who have gone forth on such a well-proclaimed spiritual path will shine if you’re respectful and deferential toward your teachers, your preceptors, or those of an equivalent standing. This will affect people’s confidence …” After rebuking them … the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 4.3.5)
“You shouldn’t do walking meditation with your sandals on when your teachers, your preceptors, or those of equivalent standing do it without. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 4.3.7)
And you shouldn’t wear sandals within a monastery. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 5.1.1)

Soon afterwards a certain monk was afflicted with a corn on his foot. The monks had to hold him while he urinated and defecated. Just then, the Buddha was walking about the dwellings and saw this. He went up to those monks and said to them, “What illness does this monk have?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 5.2.2)
“He has a corn on his foot, sir. That’s why we do this for him.” Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 5.2.5)
“I allow you to wear sandals if your feet are painful or cracked, or you have a corn on your foot.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.1.1)
Then the monks made use of the beds and benches with dirty feet. Their robes and the furniture got dirty.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.1.4)
“When you know that you are about to make use of a bed or a bench, I allow you to wear sandals.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.2.1)
Then, when the monks were walking to the observance hall or to a meeting in the dark of night, they stepped on stumps and thorns, hurting their feet.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.2.3)
“I allow you to wear sandals within a monastery, and also to use a torch, a lamp, and a walking stick.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.3.1)

At one time the monks from the group of six got up early in the morning, put on wooden shoes, and walked back and forth outside, making a loud clacking noise. And they talked about all sorts of worldly things: about kings, gangsters, and officials; about armies, dangers, and battles; about food, drink, clothes, and beds; about garlands and perfumes; about relatives, vehicles, villages, towns, and countries; about women and heroes; gossip; about the departed; about various trivialities; about the world and the sea; about being this or that. They stepped on and killed insects, and they disturbed the monks in the stillness of meditation.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.4.1)

The monks of few desires complained and criticized them, “How can the monks from the group of six act like this?” They told the Buddha. … “Is it true, monks, that the monks from the group of six are acting like this?” “It’s true, sir.” … After rebuking them … the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 6.4.12)
“You shouldn’t wear wooden shoes. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.1.1)
When the Buddha had stayed at Rājagaha for as long as he liked, he set out wandering toward Benares. When he eventually arrived, he stayed in the deer park at Isipatana.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.1.4)

When the monks from the group of six heard that the Buddha had prohibited wooden shoes, they took cuttings from young palm trees and wore shoes made of palm leaves. The trees withered. People complained and criticized them, “How can the Sakyan monastics act like this? They are harming one-sensed life.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.2.1)
The monks heard the complaints of those people and they told the Buddha. … “Is it true, monks, that the monks from the group of six are acting like this?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.2.5)
“It’s true, sir.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.2.6)

The Buddha rebuked them … “How can those foolish men have cuttings made from young palm trees and wear shoes made of palm leaves, with the trees withering as a consequence? People regard trees as conscious. This will affect people’s confidence …” After rebuking them … the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.2.13)
“You shouldn’t wear shoes made of palm leaves. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.3.1)

When they heard that the Buddha had prohibited shoes made of palm leaves, the monks from the group of six had cuttings made from young bamboo and wore shoes made of bamboo leaves. The bamboo withered. People complained and criticized them, “How can the Sakyan monastics act like this? They are harming one-sensed life.” The monks heard the complaints of those people and they told the Buddha. … “… People regard trees as conscious …
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 7.3.12)
You shouldn’t wear shoes made of bamboo leaves. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.1.1)
When the Buddha had stayed at Benares for as long as he liked, he set out wandering toward Bhaddiya. When he eventually arrived, he stayed in the Jātiyā Grove.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.1.4)

At that time the monks in Bhaddiya were fond of various kinds of nice shoes. They made shoes of grass, reed, fishtail-palm leaves, and wool, and they had them made. As a consequence, they neglected recitation, questioning, the higher morality, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. The monks of few desires complained and criticized them, “How can the monks in Bhaddiya do this?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.2.3)
They told the Buddha. … “Is it true, monks, that the monks in Bhaddiya do this?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.2.6)
“It’s true, sir.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.2.7)

The Buddha rebuked them … “How can those foolish men be fond of various kinds of nice shoes … and neglect recitation, questioning, the higher morality, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom? This will affect people’s confidence …” After rebuking them … the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.3.4)

“You shouldn’t wear shoes made of grass, reed, fishtail-palm leaves, or wool; or shoes made with gold, silver, gems, beryl, crystal, bronze, glass, tin, lead, or copper. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 8.3.6)

And you shouldn’t use shoes. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct. I allow three kinds of foot stands that are fixed in place and immobile: foot stands for defecating, foot stands for urinating, and foot stands for restroom ablutions.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.1.1)
When the Buddha had stayed at Bhaddiya for as long as he liked, he set out wandering toward Sāvatthī. When he eventually arrived, he stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.1.4)

At this time, the monks from the group of six would grab cattle as they were crossing the Aciravatī river—by the horns, the ears, the neck, and the tail—and they would mount their backs and, motivated by lust, would touch their genitals. They even killed a calf by submerging it. People complained and criticized them, “How can the Sakyan monastics act like this? They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.2.4)
The monks heard the complaints of those people and they told the Buddha. … “Is it true, monks …” “It’s true, sir.” … After rebuking them … the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.3.4)
“You shouldn’t grab cattle by the horns, the ears, the neck, or the tail, and you shouldn’t mount their backs. If you do mount their backs, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.3.6)
And you shouldn’t touch their genitals motivated by lust. If you do, you commit a serious offense.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.3.8)
And you shouldn’t kill a calf. If you do, you should be dealt with according to the rule.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.4.1)

At that time the monks from the group of six traveled in vehicles, sometimes pulled by a female animal with a man driving, at other times pulled by a male animal with a woman driving. People complained and criticized them, “You’d think they were at the Ganges festival!” They told the Buddha.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 9.4.5)
“You shouldn’t travel in a vehicle. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.1.1)

Soon afterwards a monk who was traveling through the Kosalan country on his way to visit the Buddha at Sāvatthī became sick. He stepped off the path and sat down at the foot of a tree. People saw him and said to him, “Venerable, where are you going?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.1.5)
“I’m going to Sāvatthī to visit the Buddha.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.2.1)
“Please come with us.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.2.2)
“I can’t. I’m sick.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.2.3)
“Then please come inside the vehicle.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.2.4)
“Thank you, but the Buddha has prohibited us from traveling in vehicles.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.2.5)
He did not accept because he was afraid of wrongdoing. Then, when he arrived at Sāvatthī, he told the monks what had happened. They in turn told the Buddha.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.2.7)
“I allow a vehicle when you’re sick.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.3.1)
The monks thought, “Pulled by a female or by a male?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.3.4)
“I allow a rickshaw pulled by men.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.3.5)
Soon afterwards a certain monk was even more uncomfortable when jolted around in a vehicle.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.3.7)
“I allow a palanquin and a litter.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.4.1)

At that time the monks from the group of six used high and luxurious beds, such as: high couches, luxurious couches, long-fleeced woolen rugs, multi-colored woolen rugs, white woolen rugs, red woolen rugs, cotton-down quilts, woolen rugs decorated with the images of predatory animals, woolen rugs with long fleece on one side, woolen rugs with long fleece on both sides, sheets of silk embroidered with gems, silken sheets, woolen rugs like a dancer’s rug, elephant-back rugs, horse-back rugs, carriage-seat rugs, rugs made of black antelope hide, exquisite sheets made of kadalī-deer hide, seats with canopies, seats with red cushions at each end. When people walking about the dwellings saw this, they complained and criticized them, “They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!” They told the Buddha.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.5.1)

“You shouldn’t use high and luxurious beds, such as: high couches, luxurious couches, long-fleeced woolen rugs, multi-colored woolen rugs, white woolen rugs, red woolen rugs, cotton-down quilts, woolen rugs decorated with the images of predatory animals, woolen rugs with long fleece on one side, woolen rugs with long fleece on both sides, sheets of silk embroidered with gems, silken sheets, woolen rugs like a dancer’s rug, elephant-back rugs, horse-back rugs, carriage-seat rugs, rugs made of black antelope hide, exquisite sheets made of kadalī-deer hide, seats with canopies, seats with red cushions at each end. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.6.1)

Soon afterwards when the monks from the group of six heard that the Buddha had prohibited high and luxurious beds, they used luxurious skins: lionskins, tiger skins, and leopard skins. They cut them to fit their beds and benches, and used them both there and elsewhere. When people walking about the dwellings saw this, they complained and criticized them, “They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!” They told the Buddha.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.6.8)
“You shouldn’t use luxurious skins: lionskins, tiger skins, or leopard skins. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.7.1)

Soon afterwards when the monks from the group of six heard that the Buddha had prohibited luxurious skins, they used cattle hides. They cut them to fit their beds and benches, and used them both there and elsewhere.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.7.5)

At this time a certain bad monk was associating with the family of a bad lay follower. One morning that monk robed up, took his bowl and robe, and went to that lay follower’s house, where he sat down on the prepared seat. The lay follower approached the monk, bowed, and sat down.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.8.1)

At that time that lay follower had a beautiful young calf with variegated hide, just like a young leopard. When the bad monk stared at that calf, the lay follower asked him why. He replied, “I need the skin of that calf.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.8.6)

The bad lay follower then slaughtered the calf, skinned it, and gave the skin to the bad monk. The monk hid the skin under his outer robe and left. The mother-cow, longing for her calf, followed behind him. When the monks asked him why, he said he did not know. But his outer robe was smeared with blood, and so they said, “What happened to your outer robe?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.9.8)
When he told them what had happened, they asked, “So did you encourage someone to kill?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.9.10)
“Yes.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.9.11)

The monks of few desires complained and criticized him, “How can a monk encourage someone to kill? Hasn’t the Buddha in many ways criticized killing and praised abstention from killing?” They then told the Buddha.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.10.1)
Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and questioned that bad monk: “Is it true, monk, that you encouraged someone to kill?”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.10.3)
“It’s true, sir.” …
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.10.4)

“Foolish man, how can you encourage someone to kill? Haven’t I in many ways criticized killing and praised abstention from killing? This will affect people’s confidence …” After rebuking him, the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.10.7)
“You shouldn’t make others kill. If you do, you should be dealt with according to the rule.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.10.9)
And you shouldn’t use cattle hide. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 10.10.11)
And you shouldn’t use any kind of skin. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 11.1.1)
At that time people’s beds and benches were upholstered and covered with skin. Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not sit on them.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 11.1.4)
“I allow you to sit down on what belongs to a householder, but not to lie down on it.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 11.1.5)
The dwellings were held together by straps of leather. Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not sit down.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 11.1.8)
“I allow you to sit down against a mere binding made of skin.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 12.1.1)

At that time the monks from the group of six entered the village wearing sandals. People complained and criticized them, “They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!” They told the Buddha.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 12.1.5)
“You shouldn’t enter the village wearing sandals. If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 12.1.7)
Soon afterwards a certain sick monk was unable to go to the village without sandals.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 12.1.9)
“I allow sick monks to enter the village wearing sandals.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.1.1)
At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in Avantī on Papataka Hill at Kuraraghara. At that time the lay follower Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa was his supporter.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.1.3)

On one occasion Soṇa went to Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down, and said, “Venerable, the way I understand your teaching, it’s not easy for one who lives at home to lead the spiritual life perfectly complete and pure as a polished conch shell. I wish to cut off my hair and beard, put on the ocher robes, and go forth into homelessness. Please give me the going forth.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.2.1)

“It’s difficult, Soṇa, to live the spiritual life all one’s life, eating one meal a day and sleeping by oneself. So follow the Buddhas’ instruction while remaining as a householder. At suitable times you can eat one meal a day, sleep by yourself, and abstain from sexuality.” As a result, Soṇa’s intention to go forth died down.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.2.4)
A second time Soṇa asked Mahākaccāna for the going forth, but got the same response. A third time he asked for the going forth and Mahākaccāna finally relented.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.2.11)

At that time in the southern region of Avantī, there were few monks. Only after three years, with much trouble and difficulty, was Mahākaccāna able to gather a sangha of ten monks from here and there to give the full ordination to Venerable Soṇa.
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.3.1)

After completing the rainy-season residence, Soṇa was reflecting in private: “I’ve heard that the Buddha is like this and like that, but I haven’t seen this for myself. If my preceptor allows me, I shall go and visit the Buddha, the Perfected One, the fully Awakened One.”
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.3.3)

Coming out from seclusion, Soṇa went to Mahākaccāna, bowed, sat down, and told him what he had thought. Mahākaccāna said, “Well thought, Soṇa! Please go and visit the Buddha, the Perfected and fully Awakened One. You will see someone who is pleasing to the eye and inspiring confidence; who is peaceful in mind and faculties; who is attained to the supreme subduing and calm; who is tamed, guarded, and restrained in his senses—a great being. Then, Soṇa, in my name, pay respect with your head at the Buddha’s feet and say, ‘Sir, my preceptor, Venerable Mahākaccāna, pays respect with his head at the Buddha’s feet.’ And then say this:
1. The account of Soṇa Koḷivisa, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd5 13.5.5)

‘In the southern region of Avantī, sir, there are few monks. 1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 1.1.1)

At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. At that time the monks were afflicted with autumn illness, and they could keep down neither congee nor other food. As a result, they became thin, haggard, and pale, with veins protruding all over their bodies. The Buddha noticed this and asked Venerable Ānanda why they were looking so sickly. Ānanda told him.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 1.2.1)

Then, while reflecting in private, the Buddha thought, “What tonics might I allow the monks that are generally regarded as tonics, would serve as nourishment, but aren’t considered substantial food?” It then occurred to him, “There are these five tonics— ghee, butter, oil, honey, and syrup— that are generally regarded as tonics, serve as nourishment, but aren’t considered substantial food. Why don’t I allow them these five tonics, to be received and consumed before midday?”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 1.3.1)
In the evening, when the Buddha had come out from seclusion, he gave a teaching and then told the monks what he had thought, adding:
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 1.3.11)
“I allow these five tonics, to be received and consumed before midday.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 1.4.1)

The monks then received and consumed the five tonics before midday. But even ordinary food did not agree with them, let alone greasy food. As a result of both the autumn illness and the food not agreeing with them, they became even more thin, haggard, and pale. Once again the Buddha noticed this and asked Venerable Ānanda why they were looking even worse. Ānanda told him. The Buddha then gave a teaching, and addressed the monks:
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 1.5.5)
“I allow the five tonics to be received and consumed both before and after midday.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 2.1.1)
At that time the sick monks needed fat as a tonic. They told the Buddha.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 2.1.3)

“I allow these fats as tonics: bear fat, fish fat, alligator fat, pig fat, and donkey fat. They should be received, melted, and mixed with oil before midday, and then used. If you receive, melt, and mix them with oil after midday, and then use them, you commit three offenses of wrong conduct. If you receive them before midday, but melt and mix them with oil after midday, and then use them, you commit two offenses of wrong conduct. If you receive and melt them before midday, but mix them with oil after midday, and then use them, you commit one offense of wrong conduct. If you receive, melt, and mix them with oil before midday, and then use them, there is no offense.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 3.1.1)
At that time the sick monks needed medicinal roots.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 3.1.3)

“I allow these medicinal roots: turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, white sweet flag, atis root, black hellebore, vetiver root, nut grass, and whatever other medicinal roots there are that don’t serve as fresh or cooked food. After receiving them, you may keep them for life and use them when there’s a reason. If you use them when there’s no reason, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 3.2.1)

1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.17)
I allow tubes made of bone, ivory, horn, reed, bamboo, wood, resin, fruit, metal, or shell.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.18)
At that time the tubes were not covered. Insects crawled inside of them.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.20)
“I allow a lid.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.21)
At that time the monks carried the tubes in their hands.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.23)
“I allow a bag for the tubes.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.24)
The tubes scratched each other.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.26)
“I allow a bag with two compartments.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.27)
They did not have a shoulder strap.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 13.2.29)
“I allow a shoulder strap and a string for fastening it.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.1)
At one time Venerable Pilindavaccha had a certain disease. The doctors said he needed a heated concoction of oil.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.5)
“I allow a heated concoction of oil.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.6)
They wanted to add alcohol to that concoction.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.8)
“I allow alcohol in a heated concoction of oil.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.9)
Soon afterwards the monks from the group of six heated oil with too much alcohol. They drank it and became drunk.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.11)
“You shouldn’t drink heated oil with too much alcohol. If you do, you should be dealt with according to the rule.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.1.13)
I allow you to drink heated oil if there is no discernible color, smell, or taste of alcohol.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.2.1)
The monks had heated much oil with too much alcohol. They did not know what to do with it.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.2.4)
“I allow you to determine it for external use.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.2.5)
Pilindavaccha had more heated oil, but there was no vessel for storing it.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.2.7)
“I allow three kinds of vessels: made of metal, made of wood, made of fruit.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.1)
At that time Pilindavaccha had arthritis of the hands and feet.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.3)
“I allow treatment through sweating.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.4)
He did not get better.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.6)
“I allow sweating with herbs.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.7)
He still did not get better.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.9)
“I allow heavy sweating.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.10)
He still did not get better.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.12)
“I allow hemp water.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.13)
He still did not get better.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.3.15)
“I allow a bathtub.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.1)
Pilindavaccha had arthritis.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.3)
“I allow bloodletting.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.4)
He did not get better.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.6)
“I allow bloodletting and receiving it in a horn.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.7)
Pilindavaccha had cracked feet.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.9)
“I allow salve for the feet.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.10)
He did not get better.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.12)
“I allow you to make foot salve.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.13)
At that time a monk was afflicted with abscesses.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.15)
“I allow surgery.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.16)
They needed bitter water.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.18)
“I allow bitter water.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.19)
They needed sesame paste.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.4.21)
“I allow sesame paste.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.1)
They needed flour paste.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.3)
“I allow flour paste.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.4)
They needed a dressing.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.6)
“I allow a dressing.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.7)
The sore was itching.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.9)
“I allow you to sprinkle it with mustard powder.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.10)
The sore festered.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.12)
“I allow you to fumigate it.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.13)
The flesh protruded.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.15)
“I allow you to cut it with a razor.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.16)
The sore did not heal.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.18)
“I allow oil for the sore.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.19)
The oil dripped off.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.5.21)
“I allow a bandage and all treatments for sores.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.1)
On one occasion a certain monk was bitten by a snake.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.3)
“I allow you to give him the four foul edibles: feces, urine, ash, and clay.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.5)
The monks thought, “Do they need to be received or not?”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.8)
“They should be received if there is an attendant. If there isn’t, I allow you to take them yourself and then eat them.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.9)
On one occasion a monk had drunk poison.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.11)
“I allow you to give him feces to drink.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.12)
The monks thought, “Does it need to be received or not?”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.6.15)
“I allow the one who is excreting it to receive it. When he’s received it, it doesn’t need to be received again.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.1)
On one occasion a monk was sick from a drug.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.3)
“I allow him to drink mud from a plow.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.4)
On one occasion a certain monk had indigestion.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.6)
“I allow him to drink lye.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.7)
On one occasion a certain monk suffered from jaundice.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.9)
“I allow him to drink chebulic myrobalan soaked in cattle urine.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.10)
On one occasion a certain monk suffered from a skin disease.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.12)
“I allow you to make a scented ointment.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.13)
On one occasion a monk’s body was full of impurities.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.15)
“I allow him to drink a purgative.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.16)
He needed clear congee.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.18)
“I allow clear congee.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.19)
He needed mung-bean broth.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.21)
“I allow mung-bean broth.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.22)
He needed oily mung-bean broth.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.24)
“I allow oily mung-bean broth.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.25)
He needed meat broth.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 14.7.27)
“I allow meat broth.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.1.1)

At one time Venerable Pilindavaccha was having a hillside cleared near Rājagaha, intending to build a shelter. Just then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha went to Pilindavaccha, bowed, sat down, and said, “Venerable, what are you having made?”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.1.5)
“I’m clearing the hillside, great king. I want to build a shelter.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.1.6)
“Do you need a monastery worker?”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.1.7)
“The Buddha hasn’t allowed monastery workers.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.1.8)
“Well then, sir, please ask the Buddha and tell me the outcome.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.1.9)
“Yes.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.2.1)

Pilindavaccha instructed, inspired, and gladdened King Bimbisāra with a teaching, after which the king got up from his seat, bowed down, circumambulated Pilindavaccha with his right side toward him, and left.
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.2.3)

Soon afterwards Pilindavaccha sent a message to the Buddha: “Sir, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha wishes to provide a monastery worker. What should I tell him?” The Buddha then gave a teaching and addressed the monks:
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.2.7)
“Monks, I allow monastery workers.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.3.1)
Once again King Bimbisāra went to Pilindavaccha, bowed, sat down, and said, “Sir, has the Buddha allowed monastery workers?”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.3.4)
“Yes, great king.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.3.5)
“Well then, I’ll provide you with a monastery worker.”
1. Discussion of the five tonics, Vinaya Pitaka (pli-tv-kd6 15.3.6)

Yet after making this promise, he forgot, and only remembered after a long time. He then addressed the official in charge of practical affairs: “Listen, has the monastery worker I promised been provided?”
